body: A woman sets out her tomatoes at the edge of a market at ten past six and props a phone against the scales, a crack running corner to corner across the glass. The phone is four years old and it was not new when she got it. She opens a page she saved last month, presses one thing, and a station starts — a song, then a voice saying something short between songs, then another song. She does not touch it again all morning. When a customer asks her what that is she turns the phone round so he can see the number on the screen, and he writes it on the back of his hand.

Nothing about that morning is remarkable except the part that used to be impossible. She is a very long way outside anybody’s coverage map, and she is listening to a station with a permanent number, a published schedule and a host.

A terrestrial transmitter has a horizon. Whatever a broadcaster spends, there is a ring on the map beyond which the signal simply is not, and everyone outside that ring is somebody else’s problem. This band has no horizon, and that is the single biggest thing it changes.

It is worth taking the word horizon literally for a moment, because a coverage map is a picture of two things at once. Wattage and terrain draw the outer edge of it. A licence draws the rest. A transmitter has to stand somewhere, and the somewhere has a government, and the government has a view about who may say what on which frequency and in which language. So the ring is not really a fact about distance. It is a record of who was allowed. Whole languages have sat just outside a ring for decades, not because the physics defeated anybody, but because the paperwork did, and paperwork is much harder to raise money against than a mast.
46 of the 121 assigned frequencies on this dial are playing at this moment, and every one of them reaches exactly as far as every other one, which is to say as far as there is a signal.

Serving them that way costs something, and it costs most in the places least likely to pay it back. The audio and the artwork come from a global edge network rather than from one machine in one country, so a listener in Nairobi or Manila is served from somewhere near Nairobi or Manila instead of waiting on a rack in another hemisphere. Every one of those listeners costs money to serve and none of them is being billed. Free at the point of listening is a small detail where everyone has a card on file, and an enormous one everywhere else.

The ordinary shape of digital ministry now is an application, and an application has a horizon of its own that nobody thinks to draw. It needs a store, and a store has a country list, and a country list is a licence wearing different clothes. It needs an operating system recent enough to be supported, and storage the phone may not have, and a person willing to install something on a device they share with two other people. Every one of those is a ring on a map. They are simply not printed anywhere.

So there is no application to install here and no store to be removed from. A browser and a link is the whole requirement, and the site is built deliberately to survive a slow connection and a five-year-old handset, because that is the device most of the world is actually holding. It also means a station can be handed from one person to another as a message, rather than as an instruction to go and download something first and come back afterwards.
That difference sounds like a technical preference. It is not one.

It is worth being fair to the app, because an app is genuinely better at almost everything. It can cache audio for the underground and the long flight. It can wake a phone up for the start of a programme. It survives a dead connection, it feels quicker, and it puts an icon on a screen where a bookmark gets lost. Anybody choosing on the merits, in a wealthy country, on a good connection, should probably choose the app. But an app is a thing you are permitted to have, in a country where somebody registered it, on hardware new enough to run it. The moment any one of those fails, it is not a worse experience. It is no experience at all.
A link crosses a border. An app asks permission at it.

A young man on a building site in a cold country eats his lunch in the van with the door open and sends his mother a message with six characters in it and nothing else: HM 311.50. She is most of a day away and it is already evening where she is. Neither of them mentions it afterwards. But on the Sunday when he rings her the same station is on behind her, quietly, and neither of them turns it down, and they talk for forty minutes over the top of it.

He did not send her a file, or a link she would have had to trust, or an instruction to install anything. He sent her a number, and the number meant the same thing in her kitchen as it did in his van. That is what a broadcast band is, and it is the first time one has worked at that distance.

The honest cost is that a stream is not a transistor radio, and blurring that would be dishonest. It needs data, and data is not free anywhere. On a genuinely thin connection it will stall, and a stall in the middle of a song is worse than static, because static at least keeps going. When the power fails there is nothing to fall back on, and a battery set on a shelf in the next room will still be playing whatever the mast in the next valley is sending.

But the comparison is not between a stream and a perfect radio. It is between a stream and silence, because the mast in the next valley was never going to carry her language, and the set on the shelf can only receive what somebody with a licence decided to transmit. A radio that never stalls and never plays anything you came for is not the better option. What is actually being weighed is a station that occasionally buffers against a station that does not exist.

So the absence of a horizon is not a technical boast, and it is not the interesting part on its own. It is what makes the rest of this band mean anything. A permanent frequency is worth very little if it can only be reached inside one ring on one map, and a number handed from a market stall to the back of a stranger’s hand is worth a great deal, because it will work when he gets home.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 assigned frequencies. What is on them comes in four kinds: music, which is most of the band; teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened rather than sung; family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it; and 40 international frequencies carrying 29 languages besides English, hosted in those languages rather than translated into them afterwards. All of it is reachable from the same page, on the same hardware, at the same distance, which is none.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 311.50 — Riddim and Rhyme. It is Zariah’s Afro-Caribbean catalogue, reggae and dancehall and soca and Afrobeats married to teaching hymnody and gospel-soul, and it is the right station for this particular argument because it is music that already crossed every border it was never given permission to cross. That sound travelled by ship, by cassette, by cousins, and it arrived everywhere without a licence. Putting it on a band with no horizon is not a novelty. It is the first time the delivery has matched the music.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies are being reached for and from where, which is how the next one gets placed.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 311.50 on this afternoon while you are doing something else, and let it run. Then send the number — just the number, six characters, nothing attached — to one person who is a long way from you, and see whether it works where they are. It will. That is the entire claim of this article, and it takes about nine seconds to test.
